meta.audience: Readers of the record of Zeniff
meta.location: The land of Lehi-Nephi and Shilom

world_behind.title: Graded by the standard used for Israel's kings
world_behind.text: The books of Kings summarize each reign in a single formula before narrating any of it, and measure every successor against a predecessor. This record has been doing the same since Mosiah 6, and both times the comparison is to a father rather than to David.

world_behind.title: A fifth, where a tenth was the warning
world_behind.text: Samuel told Israel that a king would take a tenth of their seed and their vineyards and give it to his officers. Noah takes a fifth of gold, silver, ziff, copper, brass, iron, fatlings, and grain. The record has already shown a king who took nothing and will show a tribute of one half.

world_behind.title: Ziff
world_behind.text: A metal named twice, both times in this chapter, and nowhere else in scripture. Like the two crops in Mosiah 9, it comes through the translation unrendered, a word the process apparently had no English equivalent for.

world_behind.title: A priestly purge
world_behind.text: Verse 5 has Noah deposing every priest his father consecrated and installing men "lifted up in the pride of their hearts." Replacing a religious establishment wholesale is a political act, and the record reports it as the first thing he did with the office.

world_behind.title: Furniture built for lying
world_behind.text: Verse 11 describes a breastwork set before the high priests' seats so they could rest their bodies and their arms on it while speaking lying and vain words. The record almost never describes interior fittings. It describes this one, and gives the reason it was built.

world_behind.title: Pharaoh's question
world_behind.text: "Who is the Lord, that shall bring upon my people such great affliction?" Pharaoh asked the same thing of Moses: who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice. The record puts Egypt's line in the mouth of a Nephite king facing his own prophet.

world_behind.title: Nineveh, and the alternative
world_behind.text: Abinadi's terms are repentance in sackcloth and ashes. That is what the king of Nineveh did, and his city was spared. Noah is offered the same exit in the same costume and hardens his heart instead.

words.text: A secondary wife, lawful in the world the Bible describes and not in this one. Jacob had already told the Nephites that the many wives and concubines of David and Solomon were abominable before God, and in this record the word never appears except under that judgment. Noah keeps them. So do his priests, which verse 4 mentions in the course of listing what the fifth part of everything was spent on.

Animals fattened for slaughter, the best of a herd. Their appearance in a tax list means the levy took the choicest stock rather than a share of the ordinary. It is a small word doing precise work about what a fifth part actually cost a farmer.

Decorated, and used three times in four verses. The objects are buildings, the palace, and the high priests' seats. The verb attaches to gold, silver, and precious things every time. What the taxes bought is described almost entirely in terms of surfaces.

Not a Bible word. In this record it belongs to Lehi's dream, where the great and spacious building stands in the air above the earth and is filled with people pointing at those who reached the tree. Noah's buildings are the first place the adjective lands outside that vision, and it lands once more a verse later, on his palace. The word paired with it here, elegant, occurs nowhere else in scripture. One other king in the record builds spacious buildings: Riplakish, in Ether, who also had many wives and concubines and paid the builders out of heavy taxes.

A place people go to, in the older sense of a refuge rather than a destination. The hill where Noah builds a great tower had been a resort for the children of Nephi when they fled. He puts a monument on a place of hiding, and the record notes the history without comment.

A habitual drinker. It is the charge Proverbs warns against and the insult leveled at Jesus by his critics. Applied to Noah it follows directly from his own vineyards and wine-presses. He built the supply and then became its customer, and his people with him.

phrases.term: He did not walk in the ways of his father
phrases.text: The whole reign summarized before a single act of it is described. The record used the same construction of Mosiah in the affirmative five chapters earlier. Nothing after this sentence is a surprise, and nothing in it is presented as one.

phrases.term: A fifth part of their ziff, and of their copper, and of their brass
phrases.text: An eight-item levy, listed without pause: gold, silver, ziff, copper, brass, iron, fatlings, grain. The completeness is the point. Nothing a person owned was outside it, and one of the eight is a substance the reader cannot identify.

phrases.term: Thus did the people labor exceedingly to support iniquity
phrases.text: The sentence that names the arrangement. The priests' laziness, idolatry, and whoredoms are funded by other people's work, and the verb given to the taxpayers is labor exceedingly. It is the record's sharpest statement about who pays for a corrupt establishment.

phrases.term: They were deceived by the vain and flattering words of the king and priests
phrases.text: The people become idolatrous by persuasion. Flattery is the named instrument, as it was with Sherem four books earlier, and the record consistently treats pleasing speech as the delivery mechanism for error.

phrases.term: That they might rest their bodies and their arms upon while they should speak lying and vain words
phrases.text: Comfort and falsehood joined by a piece of carpentry. The breastwork exists so that lying can be done at leisure. Nothing else in the record supplies a physical detail this damning, and it is delivered without any adjective of judgment attached.

phrases.term: A very high tower, even so high that he could stand upon the top thereof and overlook the land
phrases.text: Built near the temple, and used for surveillance. Noah can see Shilom, Shemlon, and all the land round about, and the same tower will be where he sees the Lamanites coming and where he is finally trapped. The record builds the instrument of his watching and then of his exposure.

phrases.term: He placed his heart upon his riches
phrases.text: The verb is deliberate: placed, not drifted. Verse 14 pairs it with riotous living, the same phrase Luke gives the prodigal in a far country. Noah is not described as losing his way; he is described as choosing where to put something.

phrases.term: Saying that their fifty could stand against thousands of the Lamanites
phrases.text: A boast with a number in it, following one successful skirmish. The record supplies the arithmetic so the reader can watch it fail later. What is being boasted in is stated plainly in the same verse: their own strength.

phrases.term: Am a jealous God, visiting the iniquities of my people
phrases.text: The Sinai formula, with one word changed. Exodus has God visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children; Abinadi has him visiting the iniquities of my people. The generational clause is dropped and the possessive is kept.

phrases.term: When they shall cry unto me I will be slow to hear their cries
phrases.text: A promise about silence. What is promised is a slow hearing, harder to endure than a refusal. Mosiah 21 will report this fulfilled in exactly these terms, and the reader who remembers this sentence will recognize it there.

phrases.term: Except they repent in sackcloth and ashes
phrases.text: The exit is named and it has a precedent. A king in sackcloth on ashes saved Nineveh in a single chapter of Jonah. Abinadi offers the same terms to a king with a spacious palace and a gold-ornamented throne. In that setting the offer feels impossible.

phrases.term: Who is Abinadi, that I and my people should be judged of him, or who is the Lord
phrases.text: Two questions, and the second is Pharaoh's. Noah moves from dismissing the messenger to dismissing the sender in the space of one sentence, which is the shortest route from irritation to defiance anyone in the record takes.

phrases.term: The eyes of the people were blinded; therefore they hardened their hearts
phrases.text: Cause and effect in that order, blindness first and hardening second. The chapter ends by making the people's part passive and their response active, and gives the king the same verb in the next clause with no mitigation at all.

verses.label: v. 1–7
verses.title: A new reign, and what it cost
verses.text: The kingdom conferred, the verdict delivered in the first sentence, many wives and concubines, a fifth part of everything taxed, the old priests deposed and proud ones installed, and a people laboring to support the whole arrangement, persuaded into it by flattery.

verses.label: v. 8–13
verses.title: What the money built
verses.text: Elegant and spacious buildings ornamented in gold and silver and ziff; a spacious palace with a throne; fine work inside the temple walls; gilded seats for the high priests with a breastwork to lean on while they lied; a very high tower by the temple for looking out over two lands; and a great tower on the hill where refugees once hid.

verses.label: v. 14–15
verses.title: How he spent his time
verses.text: His heart placed on his riches, riotous living with wives and concubines, priests with harlots, vineyards planted, wine-presses built, wine in abundance, and a king who became a wine-bibber and took his people with him.

verses.label: v. 16–19
verses.title: Raids, a victory, and a boast
verses.text: Lamanites picking off farmers and shepherds; guards sent but too few; armies sent and the enemy driven back for a time; spoil taken; and then pride, a boast about fifty against thousands, and a delight in the shedding of their brethren's blood, traced by the record to the king and priests.

verses.label: v. 20–25
verses.title: Abinadi
verses.text: A man among them, named at last, going forth with a message that is all conditions: except they repent, anger, bondage, affliction; they shall know I am the Lord and a jealous God; none shall deliver them but the Lord; their cries will be slow to be heard; and only sackcloth and ashes and mighty crying will change it.

verses.label: v. 26–27
verses.title: Two angers
verses.text: The people are wroth and try to kill him, and the Lord delivers him. The king hears and is also wroth, and asks who Abinadi is that he should judge, and who the Lord is that he should afflict.

verses.label: v. 28–29
verses.title: The order, and the hardening
verses.text: Bring him here that I may slay him, on the charge of stirring the people to contention. Then the closing sentence: the people's eyes blinded, their hearts hardened, a manhunt begun, and a king who would not repent.

chapter.title: The verdict comes before the evidence
chapter.text: Verse 1 grades the reign in the formula the books of Kings use, and the twenty-eight verses after it are the supporting file. The record is not discovering that Noah was bad; it is documenting a conclusion it states up front.

chapter.title: Corruption is described as an economy
chapter.text: A fifth part taxed, priests supported, buildings ornamented, vineyards planted, wine made. Every item of wickedness in the chapter has a funding line attached to it, and verse 6 names the arrangement outright: the people labored exceedingly to support iniquity.

chapter.title: The taxation scale runs across the whole book
chapter.text: Benjamin took nothing and worked with his own hands; Noah takes a fifth; the Lamanites will exact one half from Noah's grandchildren's generation. The record lets the reader do that arithmetic without ever assembling it.

chapter.title: The most damning detail is a piece of furniture
chapter.text: A ledge built so that men could lean on it while speaking lies. The record supplies the measurement of the corruption, and the effect is worse than any adjective would be.

chapter.title: Noah reaches Pharaoh's question immediately
chapter.text: He asks who Abinadi is, and then who the Lord is. The first is a question about standing; the second is the one Egypt asked Moses. Nothing in the chapter marks the escalation, and the reader is left to hear it.

chapter.title: The way out is named, and it has a precedent
chapter.text: Sackcloth and ashes saved Nineveh. Abinadi offers the identical terms, and the chapter ends with a hardened heart instead. The alternative is not theoretical in this record; it is a story everyone in it could have known.

chapter.title: The chapter ends on a manhunt
chapter.text: Abinadi has delivered one message and escaped once. What closes the chapter is an order for his death and a people looking for him. The prophecy itself will not be given until he is caught.

applications.title: Ask what your spending is funding
applications.text: The people's labor supported the priests' idleness, and probably most of them did not think of it that way. Look at where your money and hours actually go, and name what they are keeping alive.

applications.title: Be suspicious of what pleases you
applications.text: The people were deceived by flattering words. When a message is unusually easy to accept, that ease is data.

applications.title: Notice the comfort built around a compromise
applications.text: Somebody made that ledge on purpose. When you find yourself arranging conditions so that something questionable is easier to sustain, the arrangement is the tell.

applications.title: Watch where you place your heart
applications.text: The verb is active. Name one thing you have deliberately set your attachment on in the last year, and ask whether you chose it or defaulted to it.

applications.title: Check the boast after the win
applications.text: One skirmish produced "fifty against thousands." After something goes well, notice what you start saying about yourself, and discount it.

applications.title: Take the exit while it is offered
applications.text: Sackcloth and ashes worked for a city that had less warning than Noah did. Whatever correction you have been given, the terms do not usually improve with delay.

questions.text: If someone graded my life in one sentence before hearing the details, what would it say?
Whose labor supports something of mine that I have not examined?
What am I believing mainly because of how it was said to me?
Where have I placed my heart, and did I decide that on purpose?
Have I ever experienced God as slow to hear, and did I ask why?
When corrected, do I go after the messenger, and how fast do I get from there to dismissing the message?
